title: Functions, scope and closures
intro: Functions let you package behaviour into reusable pieces, while scope controls which variables are available where. In this lesson, you will learn how functions work, how callbacks and closures make JavaScript powerful, and why these ideas appear everywhere in React applications.
takeaways: Functions package reusable behaviour and can be declared, stored in variables, or written as arrow functions.
Parameters receive input, return values provide results, and rest parameters let a function accept many arguments.
Functions are values, so they can be passed around as callbacks to array methods, event handlers, and React components.
Closures let a function remember variables from its surrounding scope, which makes private state and independent counters possible.
Pure functions avoid external side effects, while arrow functions capture this from their surrounding scope instead of creating their own.

quiz.question: Which expression correctly defines an arrow function that receives two numbers and returns their sum?
options: const add = (a, b) => a + b;
const add => (a, b) { a + b };
function => add(a, b) return a + b;
const add = function => a + b;
quiz.explanation: The first option is valid arrow function syntax. Because the body contains a single expression without curly braces, its value is returned implicitly.

quiz.question: What does the `...numbers` parameter do in this function? `function sum(...numbers) { return numbers.length; }`
options: It converts all arguments to strings
It collects the supplied arguments into an array
It limits the function to one argument
It returns the last argument
quiz.explanation: A rest parameter collects the remaining arguments into an array. Calling sum(10, 20, 30) therefore makes numbers equal to [10, 20, 30].

quiz.question: What does this code print?
options: 0, then 0
1, then 1
2, then 2
1, then 2
quiz.explanation: The returned function closes over count. The first call changes it from 0 to 1, and the second call changes the same remembered variable from 1 to 2.

quiz.question: Which statement about a pure function is correct?
options: It must always be an arrow function
It cannot have parameters
It produces the same result for the same inputs and avoids changing external state
It must always return an object
quiz.explanation: A pure function depends only on its inputs and does not modify external state. Its syntax and return type are not what make it pure.

quiz.question: What is the important difference between arrow functions and regular functions regarding `this`?
options: Regular functions cannot use this
Arrow functions create a new this for every call
Both always receive this from the global object
Arrow functions capture this from the surrounding scope
quiz.explanation: Arrow functions do not create their own this. They capture it from the surrounding lexical scope, while regular functions can receive this based on how they are called.

exercise.title: Build private counters and one-time functions
exercise.task: Implement exactly two functions: `createCounter(start = 0)` and `once(fn)`. `createCounter` must return an object containing `increment()`, `decrement()`, and `value()`; increment and decrement must return the new count, while value returns the current count. The counter value must be private, so `count` must not be a property of the returned object, and separate calls to `createCounter` must produce independent counters. `once(fn)` must return a function that calls `fn` only on its first invocation, passes all arguments to `fn`, and returns that first result on every later invocation; the tests use these exact function names.
exercise.hint: For `createCounter`, put the count variable inside the function so the returned methods close over it. For `once`, keep two private variables in the closure: one to remember whether the function has already run and another to remember its first result; use a rest parameter to forward all arguments.

tests.name: Counter changes and returns new values
tests.code: const counter = createCounter(5); return counter.increment() === 6 && counter.increment() === 7 && counter.decrement() === 6 && counter.value() === 6;

tests.name: Counters are independent and private
tests.code: const first = createCounter(10); const second = createCounter(10); first.increment(); return first.value() === 11 && second.value() === 10 && !Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(first, "count") && !Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(second, "count");

tests.name: Once calls the function only once
tests.code: let calls = 0; const fn = once((value) => { calls += 1; return value * 2; }); const first = fn(5); const second = fn(20); return first === 10 && second === 10 && calls === 1;

tests.name: Once forwards all arguments
tests.code: let received; const fn = once((a, b, c) => { received = [a, b, c]; return a + b + c; }); const result = fn(1, 2, 3); fn(10, 20, 30); return result === 6 && received.join(",") === "1,2,3";
